summary: Hillsborough has no commercial zoning — zero restaurants, zero coffee shops, zero gas stations — making it one of the few incorporated cities on the San Francisco Peninsula that is purely residential by design. This 6.2-square-mile enclave drapes over the wooded hills west of the Bayshore, with winding roads that climb through stands of eucalyptus and mature oak, offering intermittent views of the Bay from higher elevations. The median home value exceeds $2 million against a median household income above $250,000, yielding a price-to-income ratio above 8:1 — steep even by Peninsula standards, and effectively requiring substantial existing wealth or equity to purchase. With no retail or employment base of its own, Hillsborough functions as a commuter community; neighboring Burlingame and San Mateo supply dining, groceries, and daily errands, while SFO sits roughly ten minutes east, and the Caltrain corridor connects to San Francisco and Silicon Valley job centers. The climate is classic coastal-hills mild — average highs around 65°F year-round, with 8.6 hours of daily sunshine and cool nights dipping to 51°F, meaning fog fingers creep in but rarely linger past morning. Property crime runs notably high at 446 burglaries per 100,000, a figure that stands out against the otherwise low violent-crime rate. Hillsborough is, at its core, a place that traded every urban convenience for space, quiet, and proximity to a Peninsula that has everything else.
